articleTitle: Sensors based on silicon strain gauges
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Sensing Via Strain
abstract: Modern piezoresistive sensors demand a high level of accuracy, and a more exact knowledge of the mechanisms of piezoresistance is required. Theoretical calculations coupled with accurate finite element models can be used to design linear sensors.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Multiplexing methods for fibre optic strain sensors
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Sensing Via Strain
abstract: The paper briefly reviews a number of methods for multiplexing optical-fibre-based strain sensors. These are intended for application for structural monitoring, for example in aerospace composites or civil engineering structures. Particular emphasis is placed on methods for addressing arrays of sensors using acousto-optic tunable filters and optical time domain reflectometry, which have been recently developed in the authors' laboratory.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A novel non-contact strain measurement technique utilising Rayleigh waves
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Sensing Via Strain
abstract: Many devices that are used to convert a mechanical force or load to an electrical signal rely on the measurement of strain. The stress strain relationship, is one of the most fundamental concepts from the study of mechanics of materials and can be used to measure such diverse physical parameters as force, pressure, torque and acceleration. The author outlines the principle and background of a surface acoustic waves (Rayleigh waves) transducer and considers the use of such devices in a practical application. The measurement of torque in a rotating shaft is used to demonstrate many advantages of the technique.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Vibrating strain elements: compensation and application
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Sensing Via Strain
abstract: Most mechanical transducers can be represented reasonably faithfully as a second order system, if only because one pair of complex roots tends to dominate. This behaviour, depending on the circumstances, can be a help or a hindrance. Vibrating elements can be used as primary sensors for a number of physical variables (micromass, viscosity, pressure, temperature etc). They have the attraction that their performance is largely dictated by the mechanical structure, which is easily controlled. This is particularly relevant in thick film technology, which is cheap and robust, though not well controlled. The second order response is disadvantageous in many transducers as it delays the settling time before a stable measurement can be established. If this problem can be overcome, again cheap robust versions of devices such as load cells become available.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Sensing Via Strain
abstract: Transducers are used in a wide range of applications in industry. Although technology has been used to significantly improve the performance and reduce the cost of both transducers and amplifiers, the signal processing still remains predominantly analogue. Some progress has been made to design completely digital amplifiers, however there have been limitations on the frequency response due to the use of hybrid integrated circuit techniques. This changed in 1986 when HBM developed its first gate array for the DMC9012 multichannel digital amplifier system, offering 9600 samples per second, no data skew between channels and 20 bit resolution.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Capacitor bridges in the measurement of force and torque
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Sensing Via Strain
abstract: It is established that the use of capacitor bridge techniques is appropriate to the measurement of force and torque via strain. Correct electrical and electronic design avoids the problems often believed to be inherent in such techniques. The limiting practical sensitivity is at the sub-micron level and the results show that good performance is achieved through integration of the plates into the mechanical design. Potentially manufacture is simple. It is possible to use long leads with remote electronics but there is also the potential to design and build an integrated circuit which could be incorporated within the device. An additional advantage is the potential low power consumption. That of the bridge itself is effectively zero and it would be possible to design the electronics to consume very little power.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: A planar fibre optic strain sensor using micromechanical resonators fabricated from [110] silicon wafers
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Sensing Via Strain
abstract: The authors have demonstrated a planar, fibre optic/mechanical resonator strain sensor fabricated from [110] silicon. Their design has the potential for relatively simple and rapid alignment of the fibre to the sensor. Low optical power (few hundred microwatts at 830 nm) is required for excitation. With optical excitation and interrogation, the temperature sensitivity is only -20ppm/degree Centigrade whilst the strain sensitivity is around 2250 ppm/microstrain.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>

articleTitle: Transducers for ship's hull stress monitoring
publicationTitle: IEE Colloquium on Sensing Via Strain
abstract: Ship & Marine Data Systems worked with Lloyd's Register for a number of years on the development of their Voyage Data Recorder, the shipping equivalent of the aircraft 'Black Box' flight recorder. This work included measurement of hull stress, and it was thus a natural progression to the design and manufacture of a hull stress monitor. The first three stress monitor systems were designed to a specification prepared by BP Shipping Ltd, who have now fitted them in six ships, as part of a long term study of stress in VLCC's. The system design has been improved over the past four years as operational experience is gained, with changes in both hardware and software being implemented, particular attention being given to the transducers.<<ETX xmlns:mml="http://www.w3.org/1998/Math/MathML" xmlns:xlink="http://www.w3.org/1999/xlink">></ETX>
